question: What directional relationship do yellow center line markings and white lane line markings communicate?
model_answer: Direct Answer: Yellow center line markings communicate that the traffic lanes on either side of the marking carry traffic in opposite directions of travel, while white lane line markings communicate that the lanes on either side carry traffic in the same direction of travel. In short, color conveys directionality: yellow separates opposing flows and white separates same-direction flows. The specific pattern of the yellow line (broken vs. solid) further communicates whether passing across the center line is permitted or prohibited. Standards (mandatory): - "Center line pavement markings, when used, shall be the pavement markings used to delineate the separation of traffic lanes that have opposite directions of travel on a roadway and shall be yellow." - "When used, lane line pavement markings delineating the separation of traffic lanes that have the same direction of travel shall be white." - On two-lane, two-way roadways, the center line markings shall be one of the following as shown in Figure 3B-1: "A. Two-direction passing zone markings consisting of a normal width broken yellow line where crossing the center line markings for passing with care is permitted for traffic traveling in either direction; B. One-direction no-passing zone markings consisting of a double yellow line, one of which is a normal width broken yellow line and the other is a normal width solid yellow line, where crossing the center line markings for passing with care is permitted for the traffic traveling adjacent to the broken line, but is prohibited for traffic traveling adjacent to the solid line; or C. Two-direction no-passing zone markings consisting of two normal width solid yellow lines where crossing the center line markings for passing is prohibited for traffic traveling in either direction." - "Except where a reversible lane (see Section 3B.04) or a two-way left-turn lane (see Section 3B.05) is present, the center line markings on undivided two-way roadways with four or more lanes for moving motor vehicle traffic always available shall be the two-direction no-passing zone markings consisting of normal width double solid yellow lines as shown in Figure 3B-2." Options (permitted): - Solid white lane line markings may be used: on approaches to intersections to separate contiguous through lanes; to separate through traffic lanes from auxiliary lanes, such as an added uphill truck lane; and on approaches to crosswalks across multi-lane roadways. - On shared-use paths wide enough for two minimum-width lanes, a solid yellow center line may be used to separate the two directions of travel where passing or traveling to the left of the line is not permitted, and a broken yellow center line may be used where passing is permitted. Visual evidence: - [Image 1] Figure 3B-2 shows a multi-lane, two-way roadway where double solid yellow lines separate the opposing directions (arrows pointing opposite ways) while broken white lane lines separate same-direction lanes. - [Image 2] Figure 3B-3 shows three-lane, two-way applications where the yellow center line (broken/solid combinations) marks the boundary between opposing directions and white lane lines separate the two same-direction lanes. - [Image 3] Figure 3B-1 illustrates two-lane, two-way yellow center line patterns—broken, broken-plus-solid, and double solid—corresponding to passing zones, one-direction no-passing zones, and two-direction no-passing zones. - [Image 4] The full-page view of Figure 3B-2 (p.541) confirms the double yellow center line dividing opposing arrows with white lane lines between same-direction lanes, including single-lane left-turn channelization delineated by yellow lines. - [Image 5] The full-page view of Figure 3B-3 (p.542) shows both passing-permitted and passing-prohibited three-lane configurations, with yellow marking the directional divide. - [Image 6] Page 595 (Figure 3B-11) shows white lane-drop and channelizing lines separating same-direction freeway lanes, with the yellow line only at the left edge of the directional roadway. - [Image 7] Page 674 (Figure 3I-1) shows two-way streets where tubular markers supplement the yellow center line separating opposing flows and white lane lines separating same-direction lanes. Citations: - Section 3B.01 Standard §1 (p.540) - Section 3B.06 Standard §1 (p.546) - Section 3B.01 Standard §4 (p.540) - Section 3B.01 Standard §6 (p.540) - Section 3B.06 Option §8 (p.548) - Section 9E.13 Option §1 (p.1106) - Figure 3B-1 (p.540) - Figure 3B-2 (p.541) - Figure 3B-3 (p.542) - Page 582 - Page 583 - Page 595 - Page 674
gold_answer: Yellow center lines separate lanes traveling in opposite directions. White lane lines separate lanes traveling in the same direction.
